narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tips just above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. At 28.5, it sits well below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the eyes of the model. Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing; at 3.4 it actually exceeds the 3.23 average of accepted students. Your first-year law school grades (decile 1) came in third. Placing in the 5th decile instead of the 6th-decile average of accepted students added another nudge toward predicting failure.

Taken together, the lower LSAT and slightly weaker first-year performance outweighed your stronger college GPA, tipping the model just past the threshold for rejection.

What you should do next is straightforward: retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score. Improving that single factor would likely shift your predicted probability below 50% and reopen admission opportunities. Focus your preparation there first. (218 words)
